text: This case study follows one real incident from its first raw log all the way through to closure, pulling together Defender XDR, a Sentinel analytics rule, an automation rule, a playbook, and the investigation techniques from Chapter 6 — every one of them doing the job it was built for, under real time pressure instead of a lab.

9:14 AM: a Finance user clicks a phishing link and enters credentials on a fake login page — Defender for Office 365 flags it after delivery. 9:31 AM: Lesson 29's impossible-travel rule fires on that same account, signing in from a foreign IP twelve minutes after an office sign-in. Because both alerts name the same Account entity, Sentinel merges them into one multi-stage incident automatically.

At 9:32 AM, an automation rule matching the Account entity and high severity triggers a playbook before any analyst even opens the incident. It posts the case to a SOC Teams channel with severity and entities already filled in, and disables the compromised account's sign-in ability — turning a response that used to take minutes into something that runs in seconds.

At 9:35 AM an analyst opens the incident, confirms the correlation in the investigation graph and timeline, then runs a hunting query scoped to the flagged IP address — the same pattern from Lesson 30 — to check whether it touched any other account. It didn't. That one query is what confirms this stays a single-user incident instead of a wider breach.

At 9:48 AM, with the timeline confirmed and the account already disabled, the analyst closes the case as a True Positive: credential phishing leading to account compromise. The closing note states exactly what happened, what the playbook already did, and what still has to happen — password reset and MFA re-registration — before the account comes back online.

Detection, correlation, automated response, human investigation, and a clear closing note — none of it worked in isolation. The final lesson reviews every chapter that made this case study possible, from Sentinel's architecture through KQL, analytics rules, workbooks, Defender XDR, investigation, and playbooks.
